blocks.text: “Thank you, your ladyship.” Mr. Guppy does so. “Now, your ladyship—” Mr. Guppy looks at a small piece of paper. On it, he has written small notes to guide his argument. Yet whenever he looks at the paper, it seems to confuse him completely. “I—oh yes!—I put myself completely in your ladyship's hands. If your ladyship complained about this visit to Kenge and Carboy, or to Mr. Tulkinghorn, it would put me in a very unpleasant situation. I admit that openly. So I count on your ladyship's honor.”
With the hand holding the screen, my Lady makes a proud movement showing how much she looks down on him. She tells him for certain that he is not worth any complaint from her.

“Thank you, your ladyship,” says Mr. Guppy. “I am quite satisfied with that. Now—I—oh, bother! The fact is, I wrote down one or two short headings here. They show the order of the points I thought about mentioning. But I wrote them in a short form, and I cannot quite see what they mean. If your ladyship will excuse me for taking the paper to the window for half a moment, I—”

As Mr. Guppy goes to the window, he bumps clumsily into a pair of love-birds. In his confusion, he says to them, “I really beg your pardon.” This does not make his notes any easier to read. Growing warm and red in the face, he holds the piece of paper first close to his eyes, then far away. Quietly, he says to himself, “C. S. What is C. S. for? Oh! ‘E. S.’! Oh, I know! Yes, of course!” Now that everything is clear to him, he comes back.
Mr. Guppy stands halfway between my Lady and his chair. “I do not know, your ladyship,” he says, “whether you ever happened to hear of a young lady named Miss Esther Summerson, or to see her.”
My Lady's eyes look straight at him. “I saw a young lady with that name not long ago. This past autumn.”
Mr. Guppy crosses his arms and holds his head to one side, scratching the corner of his mouth with his notes. “Now, did it seem to your ladyship that she looked like anybody?” he asks.
My Lady never takes her eyes off him again.
Mr. Guppy says, “I think your ladyship can hardly remember Miss Summerson's face?”
“I remember the young lady very well. What does this have to do with me?”

“Your ladyship, I can truly tell you that Miss Summerson's image is fixed deeply in my heart. I mention this privately, trusting you to keep it secret. While I was on a short trip in the county of Lincolnshire with a friend, I had the honor of looking around your ladyship's great house, Chesney Wold. With her image in my heart, I found a very strong likeness between Miss Esther Summerson and your ladyship's own portrait. That likeness shook me completely. In fact, it shook me so much that, at the moment, I did not even know what had shaken me. Since then, I have often been bold enough to look at your ladyship in your carriage in the park. I suppose you did not know I was there. Still, I never saw your ladyship so close before. Now I have the honor of seeing your ladyship up close, and it is really more surprising than I thought.”

Young man named Guppy! There have been times when ladies lived in strongly defended castles. Ready whenever they called, they had servants who did not care about right or wrong. Suppose you had lived then, with those beautiful eyes looking at you as they look at this moment. That poor life of yours would not have been safe for even a minute.
My Lady slowly uses her little hand-screen as a fan. She asks him again what he thinks his liking for noticing how people look alike has to do with her.

Mr. Guppy looks at his paper again. “Your ladyship,” he replies, “I am coming to that. Oh, bother these notes. Oh! ‘Mrs. Chadband.’ Yes.” Mr. Guppy pulls his chair a little forward and sits down again. My Lady leans back calmly in her chair. However, she is perhaps a little less graceful and relaxed than usual. And her steady look at him never weakens. “Ah—wait a minute, though!” Mr. Guppy checks his paper again. “E. S. twice? Oh yes! Yes, I see how to go on now, straight ahead.”
